name: Leopard 2A6

cost.display: ~$9–10M per new-build unit (secondhand/refurbished transfers have run far lower, e.g. ~€2M/tank in bulk surplus deals)

key_facts.label: Protection
key_facts.value: Composite armor; add-on/anti-drone cage kits fielded in Ukraine

short_role: Western-supplied main battle tank used for direct-fire support and defensive strongpoints; more sophisticated but far less numerous than Soviet-legacy armor.
characteristics: Crew of 4 (loader, unlike autoloader-equipped Soviet-pattern tanks)
120mm smoothbore main gun, advanced fire-control and thermal sights
Composite armor plus improvised anti-drone cage kits added in the field
Small fielded numbers relative to Soviet-legacy armor mean each loss is proportionally more significant
employment_notes: The doctrine-grounded finding that matters most here isn't the tank's specs — it's who controls the air above it. With genuine local air/drone superiority, armor can push as close as roughly 1–1.5 km from the line and use direct-fire positions; without it, the same asset is pushed back to roughly 7 km and restricted to indirect/overwatch roles. Which of those two postures this tank is actually in is a bigger factor in survivability than any armor upgrade.
contrast_vs_traditional: Cold War doctrine planned massed armored breakthroughs under an assumed friendly air umbrella. Persistent drone reconnaissance has made that umbrella conditional and local rather than general — control of the lower sky, not doctrine, now sets how close a tank can sit to the line, which is a fundamentally different planning factor than anything Cold War armor doctrine accounted for.

reactive_behavior.description: On select: short movement, turret traverse, main gun fires.

Receives threat warning and target cueing from tactical reconnaissance drones.
